academy.coffee.l0.t5: Brewing methods: by pressure (espresso, moka), by immersion (French press, AeroPress) and by drip (V60, Chemex, Kalita). Each highlights different traits: body, clarity, sweetness.
academy.coffee.l0.tip3: Rule-of-thumb ratios: espresso 1:2 (18 g → 36 g), filter 1:16 (60 g per litre), French press 1:15. Tweak to your taste and the origin of the bean.
academy.coffee.l0.t6: Water is 98% of the drink. Too hard masks aromas; too soft over-extracts. Target TDS: 75–250 mg/L. Never use distilled water or heavily chlorinated tap water.
academy.coffee.l0.note3: Ideal filter brew temperature is 92–96 °C. Too cold = sour and flat; too hot = bitter and burnt. Espresso runs a touch cooler: 90–94 °C.
academy.coffee.l0.les0.q1: Which two species dominate the world coffee market?
academy.coffee.l0.les0.q1exp: Arabica (~60%) and Robusta (~40%) are the two commercial species.
academy.coffee.l0.les0.q2: What sets Arabica apart from Robusta?
academy.coffee.l0.les0.q2exp: Arabica stands out for aroma and acidity; Robusta for caffeine, bitterness and body.
academy.coffee.l0.les0.q3exp: The coffee plant is native to Ethiopia; Yemen played a key role in its early commercial spread.
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q1: Which roast preserves more acidity and nuance?
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q1exp: The lighter the roast, the more origin nuance and acidity you keep.
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q2: What grind size do you use for espresso?
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q2exp: Espresso's short, high-pressure shot needs a fine grind, but not dusty.
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q3: When is coffee at its best after roasting?
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q3a2: Same day, straight out of the roaster
academy.coffee.l0.les1.q3exp: Before 7 days the coffee is gassy; after 30 it loses aroma quickly.
academy.coffee.l0.les2.q1exp: Espresso uses about 9 bar of pressure; V60 is drip, French press is immersion.
academy.coffee.l0.les2.q2: What's the typical ratio for filter coffee?
academy.coffee.l0.les2.q2exp: 1:16 lands a balanced cup; 1:2 is espresso and 1:30 is washed out.
academy.coffee.l0.les2.q3: Which water temperature for a pourover?
academy.coffee.l0.les2.q3exp: 92–96 °C extracts balance; too hot burns, too cold leaves it sour.
academy.coffee.l1.title: Espresso and milk
academy.coffee.l1.desc: Anatomy of espresso, milk steaming and classic drinks
academy.coffee.l1.t1: Espresso is a concentrated drink brewed under pressure: about 9 bar force 90–94 °C water through 7–18 g of finely ground coffee over 25–30 seconds.
academy.coffee.l1.tip1: Classic ratio 1:2 (double espresso: 18 g of coffee → 36 g of liquid in cup). Adjust the grind so the shot takes 25–30 s at that ratio.
academy.coffee.l1.t2: Crema is the golden foam on top: it comes from oils emulsified with CO₂. Thin hazelnut crema means fresh coffee and a proper extraction; dark or missing crema signals something's off.
academy.coffee.l1.note1: Typical faults: channeling (water finds shortcuts), over-extracted shot (past 35 s, bitter: grind coarser) or fast shot (under 20 s, sour and weak: grind finer). A flat, even tamp is key.
academy.coffee.l1.t3: Steaming milk means making microfoam: heating it from 4 to 60–65 °C while introducing controlled air. The result is silky shiny milk, like liquid white paint.
academy.coffee.l1.tip2: Two phases: stretching (first 3–4 seconds with the tip near the surface) and texturing (plunge the tip to spin without adding more air). Target temperature: 60–65 °C.
academy.coffee.l1.t4: Whole milk performs best thanks to its fat and protein. Plant alternatives: barista oat (most stable), soy (neutral taste), almond and coconut need more patience because of lower protein.
academy.coffee.l1.note2: Never re-steam already-steamed milk: proteins denature and lose structure. Always start with cold milk and a cold pitcher.
academy.coffee.l1.t5: Macchiato (espresso 'marked' with a dollop of foam), cortado (espresso + milk 1:1), flat white (double ristretto + 120 ml silky milk) and latte (30 ml espresso + 180–220 ml milk).
academy.coffee.l1.tip3: The classic Italian cappuccino is 1/3 espresso, 1/3 milk, 1/3 dense foam. The Australian flat white has less foam and more liquid, with a very silky texture.
academy.coffee.l1.t6: Basic latte art: heart (pour slowly and finish high), rosetta (swing the pitcher back-and-forth, slice at the end) and tulip (stacked hearts). The secret is to pour low and close.
academy.coffee.l1.note3: Latte art won't rescue an unbalanced drink. First nail the extraction and the milk; decoration comes after.
academy.coffee.l1.les0.q1: What's the typical extraction pressure for espresso?
academy.coffee.l1.les0.q1exp: The standard is 9 bar; some machines go to 10–11, but 9 is the classic benchmark.
academy.coffee.l1.les0.q2: What ratio is typical of a classic espresso?
academy.coffee.l1.les0.q2exp: 1:2 is the 'normale' ratio; 1:5 would be lungo and 1:16 is filter.
academy.coffee.l1.les0.q3: What does a shot pulling in 15 seconds tell you?
academy.coffee.l1.les0.q3exp: A fast shot points to a coarse grind; tighten the grinder until it lands at 25–30 s.
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q1: What target temperature should steamed milk reach?
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q1exp: Over 70 °C milk scalds and loses sweetness; under 55 °C it tastes lukewarm.
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q2: When do you introduce air during steaming?
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q2a1: At the start, with the tip near the surface
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q2a2: At the end, once it's hot
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q2exp: Air goes in during the first 3–4 s; then you plunge the tip to texture without adding more.
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q3: Which plant milk tends to behave best for latte art?
academy.coffee.l1.les1.q3exp: Barista versions of oat milk add protein/fat to mimic dairy structure.
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q1: Which drink is 1/3 espresso, 1/3 milk and 1/3 foam?
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q1exp: The Italian cappuccino balances equal thirds; flat white and latte have more milk and less foam.
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q2a1: Double ristretto + silky microfoam with no dry foam
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q2a2: Lots of dense foam on top
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q2a3: Long black coffee with a splash of cream
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q2a4: Espresso topped up with hot water
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q2exp: The flat white favours silky microfoam and a stronger coffee hit; no thick foam cap.
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q3: What decides the quality of a milk-based drink most?
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q3a2: The size of the heart drawn in latte art
academy.coffee.l1.les2.q3exp: Mouthfeel and balance come first; latte art is the cherry on top, not the foundation.
academy.coffee.l2.title: Origins and processing
academy.coffee.l2.desc: The coffee map: Africa, Americas, and Asia-Pacific
academy.coffee.l2.t1: Ethiopia is the ancestral home of Arabica: thousands of heirloom varieties across regions like Yirgacheffe (floral, jasmine, bergamot), Sidamo (citrus, black tea), and Harrar (natural process, blueberry, chocolate). Wild coffee still grows in many areas.
academy.coffee.l2.tip1: Ethiopian 'heirlooms' aren't a single variety but an umbrella covering hundreds of local cultivars farmers have selected over centuries.
academy.coffee.l2.t2: Kenya means vibrant acidity: bold blackcurrant, tomato, and citrus notes from local varieties SL28 and SL34 plus a double-washed process. AA and AB grades refer to bean size.
academy.coffee.l2.note1: Other important African origins: Rwanda and Burundi (clean Bourbons with red fruit and caramel), Tanzania (Kilimanjaro, citrus and medium body), and Uganda (a major Robusta producer).
academy.coffee.l2.t3: Colombia is the world's second-largest Arabica producer: Andean farms between 1200 and 2000 m, varieties Castillo, Caturra, Typica, and Bourbon. Classic profile: medium body, clean acidity, chocolate and nuts (Huila and Nariño now yield more floral, complex profiles).
academy.coffee.l2.tip2: Brazil produces nearly a third of the world's coffee. Most of it is natural (cherries dried whole): sweet, chocolaty, nutty, low acidity. A staple for espresso blends.
academy.coffee.l2.t4: Central America features three classic jewels: Guatemala (Antigua, set among active volcanoes, and Huehuetenango: body, chocolate, and spice), Costa Rica (Tarrazú: clean, citrusy, honeyed; a pioneer of honey processing), and El Salvador (Pacamara variety, floral and complex).
academy.coffee.l2.note2: Other Latin origins to watch: Mexico (Chiapas, Oaxaca; soft profiles), Honduras (rapidly rising in quality), Nicaragua (Jinotega and Nueva Segovia), and Peru (organic Andean farms).
academy.coffee.l2.t5: Indonesia is uniquely Asian: Sumatra, processed with giling basah (wet hulled), yields dense, herbal coffees with earthy, cedar, and tobacco notes. Java and Sulawesi also stand out. Robusta leads in Vietnam.
academy.coffee.l2.tip3: Vietnam is the world's top Robusta producer: most of it goes into instant coffee and Italian espresso blends for its body and thick crema. A growing Arabica specialty niche exists in Dalat.
academy.coffee.l2.t6: Yemen has produced coffee since the 15th century with ancestral methods: terrace drying, long fermentation, powerful fermented profiles (dried fruit, wine, spices). Hawaii (Kona) grows a sweet, velvety Arabica that fetches premium prices.
academy.coffee.l2.note3: Three key processing methods: washed (clean, acidic, transparent), natural (whole cherry dried; sweet, fruity, fermented), and honey (skin off but mucilage on; in-between, juicy). Anaerobic and carbonic fermentations are today's experimental edge.
academy.coffee.l2.les0.q1: Which Ethiopian region is famous for floral and bergamot notes?
academy.coffee.l2.les0.q1exp: Yirgacheffe (Sidamo, Ethiopia) is the paradise of floral Arabicas: jasmine, bergamot, black tea.
academy.coffee.l2.les0.q2: Which varieties are associated with Kenyan coffee?
academy.coffee.l2.les0.q2exp: SL28 and SL34 were selected at Scott Laboratories (Kenya) and deliver that signature vibrant acidity.
academy.coffee.l2.les0.q3: What does the 'AA' grade indicate in Kenyan coffee?
academy.coffee.l2.les0.q3exp: AA marks large beans (screen 17–18), followed by AB, C, etc. It's a size scale, not absolute quality.
academy.coffee.l2.les1.q1: What is Brazil's main processing method?
academy.coffee.l2.les1.q1exp: Brazil is famous for the natural process: sweet, chocolaty coffees with low acidity, perfect for espresso.
academy.coffee.l2.les1.q2: Which Guatemalan region is known for volcanic, spicy coffee?
academy.coffee.l2.les1.q2exp: Antigua (flanked by active volcanoes) gives body, chocolate, and spice; Tarrazú is Costa Rican and Nariño Colombian.
academy.coffee.l2.les1.q3exp: Costa Rica popularized honey: skin is removed but mucilage stays on the bean during drying.
academy.coffee.l2.les2.q1: Which country is the world's top Robusta producer?
academy.coffee.l2.les2.q1exp: Over 95% of Vietnam's output is Robusta; the country is also the world's #2 coffee producer overall.
academy.coffee.l2.les2.q2: Which process defines Sumatra coffee's earthy, herbal profile?
academy.coffee.l2.les2.q2exp: Giling basah removes parchment at high moisture (30–50%), giving dense body, herbal and earthy notes.
academy.coffee.l2.les2.q3exp: Kona (Big Island) produces sweet, balanced, very smooth Arabica — one of the most expensive coffees in the world.
academy.coffee.l3.title: Brewing methods and cupping
academy.coffee.l3.desc: Pour over, immersion, cupping, and the flavor wheel
academy.coffee.l3.t1: Pour over: water passes through a bed of coffee and paper filter by gravity. The V60 (Hario) stands out with its cone, spiral ribs, and a single large hole: it extracts with clarity and highlights delicate aromas.
academy.coffee.l3.tip1: Base V60 recipe for one cup: 15 g coffee and 250 g water at 92–94 °C (1:16 ratio, ≈ 60 g per liter). Bloom with 30 g for 30 s, then slow circular pours to finish. Total time 2:30–3:00.
academy.coffee.l3.t2: Chemex uses thick filters, yielding very clean cups and light body (they retain most of the oils). Kalita Wave has a flat bed and three small holes: more forgiving pour, more even extraction.
academy.coffee.l3.note1: The 'bloom' is the initial swell when coffee is first wetted: it releases CO₂ trapped from roasting and stops gas from blocking extraction. It lasts 30–45 s with 2× coffee weight in water.
academy.coffee.l3.t3: Full immersion: coffee and water share the entire extraction time. French Press uses a metal mesh (full body, plenty of oils); 4-minute immersion with coarse grind. AeroPress is a gentle manual-pressure hybrid: fast, versatile, compact.
academy.coffee.l3.tip2: Italian moka isn't espresso (it works at 1–2 bar, not 9): medium-fine grind, low heat, remove at the final gurgling sound. Intense profile, gentle bitterness, creamy.
academy.coffee.l3.t4: Cold brew: cold or room-temperature water + coarse coffee steeped 12–18 hours. Results are smooth, sweet, low in acidity. Different from iced coffee (hot-brewed coffee poured over ice, brighter).
academy.coffee.l3.note2: Reference ratios: V60 and Chemex 1:16, French Press 1:15, AeroPress 1:14 (classic recipe), Italian moka filled level, cold brew 1:8 concentrate (then diluted).
academy.coffee.l3.t5: Cupping is coffee's universal SCA protocol: 8.25 g of coarsely ground coffee in a cup, 150 ml of water at 93 °C, 4 min infusion, breaking the crust with the spoon (smelling intensely), and slurping loudly to aerosolize.
academy.coffee.l3.tip3: The SCA flavor wheel groups descriptors into families: fruity (berries, citrus, dried fruit), floral (jasmine, rose), sweet (honey, caramel), nutty/cocoa, spices, roasted, fermented, green/vegetative, other.
academy.coffee.l3.t6: Attributes cuppers score (6–10 scale): fragrance/aroma, flavor, aftertaste, acidity, body, balance, uniformity, clean cup, sweetness, and overall. Total out of 100; ≥ 80 is considered specialty.
academy.coffee.l3.note3: Common defects: phenolic (medicinal, from borer beetle), nasty ferment (rotten, matchstick), mold, rancid (oxidized oils), quaker (unripe bean that didn't roast well; beige among the roasted beans).
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q1: What shape is a V60 filter?
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q1a1: Cone with a single large hole and spiral ribs
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q1a3: Cylindrical vessel with plunger and mesh
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q1exp: V60 (Hario) is a 60° cone with a single large hole; its spiral ribs allow lateral airflow.
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q2: What water:coffee ratio is typical for pour over?
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q2exp: The SCA filter reference is 55–65 g coffee per liter; 1:16 falls within it.
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q3: What is the purpose of the bloom at the start of a pour over?
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q3a1: To release trapped CO₂ from roasting
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q3a3: To cool the coffee so it doesn't turn bitter
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q3a4: To add oxygen to the brew
academy.coffee.l3.les0.q3exp: The bloom releases roast CO₂; without it, gas pushes water away and prevents even extraction.
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q1: What grind size suits French Press?
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q1exp: French Press mesh lets fines through and clouds the cup; coarse grind keeps that to a minimum.
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q2: What approximate pressure does an Italian moka pot operate at?
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q2exp: Moka works between 1 and 2 bar; it's nowhere near espresso (9 bar) even if the result is concentrated.
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q3: How does cold brew differ from iced coffee?
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q3a1: Cold brew is steeped cold for hours; iced coffee is hot coffee over ice
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q3a2: Cold brew always has milk, iced coffee doesn't
academy.coffee.l3.les1.q3exp: Cold brew = long cold infusion (smooth, sweet); iced coffee = hot brew quickly chilled (bright, more acidic).
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q1: What step is characteristic of SCA cupping?
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q1a1: Breaking the crust with a spoon and smelling intensely
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q1a4: Using steamed milk as a control
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q1exp: After 4 minutes of infusion, breaking the crust releases a burst of aromas and is an essential step.
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q2: What SCA score marks coffee as specialty?
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q2exp: 80/100 and above on the official SCA cupping form qualifies a coffee as 'specialty'.
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q3a1: An unripe bean that doesn't roast well
academy.coffee.l3.les2.q3exp: Quakers are defective (unripe) beans that stay beige among roasted ones and taste papery/cardboard-like.
academy.cocktail.l0.title: Foundations
academy.cocktail.l0.desc: Tools, techniques, base spirits, and measurements
academy.cocktail.l0.t1: Every bartender needs essential tools: a shaker, mixing glass, strainer, jigger, and bar spoon. The Boston shaker (two pieces) is preferred by professionals, while the cobbler shaker (three pieces) is ideal for beginners.
academy.cocktail.l0.tip1: Invest in a good double-sided jigger (30/60ml). Precision in measurements is the difference between a good cocktail and an extraordinary one.
academy.cocktail.l0.t2: Standard measurements: 1 oz = 30 ml, 1 dash = ~1 ml, 1 barspoon = 5 ml. Most recipes use ounces (oz) or milliliters (ml). A standard cocktail contains 60–90 ml of total alcohol.
academy.cocktail.l0.note1: In professional bartending, consistency is more important than speed. A bartender who measures precisely will always outperform one who improvises.
academy.cocktail.l0.t3: The three fundamental techniques: SHAKE for cocktails with citrus, egg, or dairy; STIR for cocktails made only with spirits and liqueurs; BUILD for highballs and long drinks directly in the glass.
academy.cocktail.l0.tip2: When shaking, shake vigorously for 10–15 seconds. The ice should sound like maracas. When stirring, rotate the spoon gently for 30–40 revolutions to dilute without breaking the ice.
academy.cocktail.l0.t4: The 6 base spirits of mixology: Gin (botanicals), Vodka (neutral), Rum (sugarcane), Tequila/Mezcal (agave), Whisky (grains), and Brandy/Cognac (grape). Each one defines entire families of cocktails.
academy.cocktail.l0.t5: Ice is an ingredient, not an accessory. Types: large cubes (slow dilution, ideal for spirit-forward), standard cubes (shaker), crushed ice (fast dilution, tiki and cobblers). Never reuse ice from the shaker.
academy.cocktail.l0.tip3: Always use fresh ice straight from the freezer. 'Wet' ice that has been sitting out will dilute your cocktail too quickly.
academy.cocktail.l0.note2: The golden rule: if the cocktail contains citrus or opaque ingredients, shake it. If it only has spirits, liqueurs, and clear bitters, stir it. Exceptions exist, but this rule covers 90% of cases.
academy.cocktail.l0.q1: What is the correct technique for a cocktail that contains lemon juice?
academy.cocktail.l0.q1exp: Cocktails with citrus are shaken to integrate and emulsify the ingredients.
academy.cocktail.l0.q2: How many milliliters are in one ounce (oz)?
academy.cocktail.l0.q2exp: One ounce equals 30 ml. It is the standard measurement in mixology.
academy.cocktail.l0.q3exp: Tequila is distilled from blue agave (Agave tequilana Weber), exclusive to certain regions of Mexico.
academy.cocktail.l0.q4: For what type of cocktails is the stirring technique used?
academy.cocktail.l0.q4exp: Stirring is used for spirit-forward cocktails without opaque ingredients, such as the Manhattan or the Negroni.
academy.cocktail.l0.q5exp: A dash is approximately 1 ml, the amount that comes out of a bitters bottle with a single shake.
academy.cocktail.l0.q6: Which shaker is preferred by professionals?
academy.cocktail.l0.q6exp: The two-piece Boston shaker (tin + glass or tin + tin) is the professional standard due to its speed and ease of cleaning.
academy.cocktail.l0.q7: What type of ice is ideal for spirit-forward cocktails like the Old Fashioned?
academy.cocktail.l0.q7exp: Large cubes dilute slowly, keeping the cocktail cold without watering it down quickly. Perfect for spirit-forward drinks.
academy.cocktail.l0.q8exp: Rum is distilled from sugarcane or its byproducts (molasses, cane juice).
academy.cocktail.l0.q9: How many revolutions are recommended when stirring a cocktail?
academy.cocktail.l0.q9exp: 30–40 gentle revolutions with the bar spoon is the standard to achieve the correct dilution and temperature.
academy.cocktail.l0.q10: How much total alcohol does a standard cocktail contain?
academy.cocktail.l0.q10exp: A standard cocktail contains 60–90 ml of total alcohol, equivalent to about 2–3 oz of spirit.
academy.cocktail.l0.les0.q1: How many pieces does a Boston shaker have?
academy.cocktail.l0.les0.q1exp: The Boston shaker has 2 pieces (tin + glass or tin + tin) and is the professional standard for its speed and ease of cleaning.
academy.cocktail.l0.les0.q2: What type of shaker is recommended for beginners?
academy.cocktail.l0.les0.q2exp: The cobbler shaker has 3 pieces (tin, strainer, cap) and is ideal for beginners because of its built-in strainer.
academy.cocktail.l0.les0.q3: What are the standard measures of a jigger?
academy.cocktail.l0.les0.q3exp: A standard jigger has two sides: 30 ml (1 oz) and 60 ml (2 oz), providing precise measurements for cocktail recipes.
academy.cocktail.l0.les1.q1: Which technique should be used for cocktails containing citrus juice?
academy.cocktail.l0.les1.q1exp: Cocktails with citrus, egg, or dairy ingredients must be shaken to integrate and emulsify the components properly.
academy.cocktail.l0.les1.q2: How long should a cocktail typically be shaken?
academy.cocktail.l0.les1.q2exp: The standard shaking time is 10-15 seconds, enough to chill and dilute the cocktail properly.
academy.cocktail.l0.les1.q3: How many base spirits are considered fundamental in mixology?
academy.cocktail.l0.les1.q3exp: The 6 base spirits are gin, vodka, rum, tequila, whisky, and brandy — the foundation of virtually all classic cocktails.
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q1: What type of ice is best for spirit-forward cocktails?
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q1exp: Large cubes dilute slowly, keeping spirit-forward cocktails cold without watering them down too quickly.
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q2: Why should you never reuse shaker ice in a cocktail?
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q2a1: It is already diluted and will over-dilute the drink
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q2a2: It changes color from the ingredients
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q2a4: It is too large to fit in the glass
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q2exp: Shaker ice has already melted and absorbed flavors during shaking. Using fresh ice in the glass ensures proper dilution control.
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q3: What is the golden rule of cocktail technique selection?
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q3a1: Citrus means shake; spirits-only means stir
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q3a4: Use the build technique for all cocktails
academy.cocktail.l0.les2.q3exp: The golden rule: if a cocktail has citrus or opaque ingredients, shake it; if it is spirits and liqueurs only, stir it.
academy.cocktail.l1.title: Highballs & Collins
academy.cocktail.l1.desc: Simple long drinks using the build technique
academy.cocktail.l1.t1: A highball is the simplest form of cocktail: a spirit + a long mixer (soda, tonic, ginger ale) served in a tall glass with ice. The technique is 'build': pour directly into the glass. The classic ratio is 1:2 or 1:3 (spirit:mixer).
academy.cocktail.l1.tip1: Always pour the mixer down the side of the glass to preserve carbonation. Never shake a highball — you would destroy the bubbles.
academy.cocktail.l1.note1: In Japan, the Highball is an art form. Hand-carved ice is used, the glass is pre-chilled, and exactly one stir of the spoon is given. Perfection lies in simplicity.
academy.cocktail.l1.t2: The highball family includes: Buck (spirit + ginger beer + citrus), Rickey (spirit + lime + soda, no sugar), Mule (spirit + ginger beer + lime), and Collins (spirit + lemon + sugar + soda). Each is a variation on the same concept.
academy.cocktail.l1.tip2: The Collins glass is narrower and taller than the Highball glass. Use a Collins glass for higher-volume drinks and a Highball glass for shorter ones.
academy.cocktail.l1.t3: The rules for the perfect highball: 1) Pre-chilled glass, 2) Ice to the top, 3) Spirit first, 4) Mixer down the side, 5) A single stir, 6) Minimal garnish. Carbonation is your friend — treat it with respect.
academy.cocktail.l1.note2: The Dark 'n' Stormy is a registered trademark of Gosling's: it can officially only be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum. It is one of the few cocktails with a protected designation.
academy.cocktail.l1.q1: What is the technique for preparing a highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.q1exp: Highballs are built directly in the glass, without a shaker or mixing glass.
academy.cocktail.l1.q2: What defines a 'Buck' within the highball family?
academy.cocktail.l1.q2exp: A Buck combines a spirit with ginger beer and a citrus element (lime or lemon).
academy.cocktail.l1.q3: What is the classic spirit:mixer ratio in a highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.q3exp: The classic ratio is 1:2 or 1:3 (one part spirit to two or three parts mixer).
academy.cocktail.l1.q4: Why is the mixer poured down the side of the glass?
academy.cocktail.l1.q4exp: Pouring down the side preserves the CO2 bubbles, keeping the drink effervescent longer.
academy.cocktail.l1.q5: What spirit does a Moscow Mule contain?
academy.cocktail.l1.q5exp: The Moscow Mule is made with vodka, ginger beer, and lime juice, traditionally served in a copper mug.
academy.cocktail.l1.q6: What sets a Rickey apart from other highballs?
academy.cocktail.l1.q6exp: The Rickey is a dry highball: spirit + lime + soda, with no sugar or sweetener of any kind.
academy.cocktail.l1.q7: Which of these is a Collins?
academy.cocktail.l1.q7exp: The Tom Collins (gin + lemon + sugar + soda) is the quintessential Collins.
academy.cocktail.l1.q8: Which brand holds the Dark 'n' Stormy as a registered trademark?
academy.cocktail.l1.q8exp: The Dark 'n' Stormy is a registered trademark of Gosling's and can officially only be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum.
academy.cocktail.l1.q9: How many stirs of the spoon are given in a Japanese highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.q9exp: In the Japanese highball technique, exactly one stir is given to integrate without losing carbonation.
academy.cocktail.l1.q10: What tequila cocktail is more popular than the Margarita in Mexico?
academy.cocktail.l1.q10exp: The Paloma (tequila + grapefruit + soda) is the most consumed tequila cocktail in Mexico.
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q1: What technique is used to prepare a highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q1a1: Build — pour directly into the glass
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q1exp: Highballs use the build technique: ingredients are poured directly into the serving glass over ice.
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q2: What is the classic spirit-to-mixer ratio in a highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q2exp: The standard highball ratio is 1 part spirit to 2 or 3 parts mixer, keeping the drink refreshing and light.
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q3: Why should you never shake a highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q3a2: It would make the drink too cold
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q3a3: It would cause the glass to crack
academy.cocktail.l1.les0.q3exp: Shaking a highball destroys the carbonation of the mixer. The mixer is poured down the side of the glass to preserve bubbles.
academy.cocktail.l1.les1.q1: What defines a Buck within the highball family?
academy.cocktail.l1.les1.q1exp: A Buck is a highball variation combining a spirit with ginger beer and a citrus element (usually lime or lemon).
academy.cocktail.l1.les1.q2: What distinguishes a Rickey from other highballs?
academy.cocktail.l1.les1.q2exp: The Rickey is a dry highball: spirit + lime + soda, with no sugar or sweetener. It is austere and refreshing.
academy.cocktail.l1.les1.q3: What spirit does the Moscow Mule use?
academy.cocktail.l1.les1.q3exp: The Moscow Mule is made with vodka, ginger beer, and lime, traditionally served in a copper mug.
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q1: What is the rule for the number of stirs in a perfect highball?
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q1exp: The perfect highball requires only a single stir to integrate without losing carbonation — especially prized in Japanese technique.
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q2: Why is the Dark 'n' Stormy a unique cocktail legally?
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q2a1: It is a registered trademark of Gosling's
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q2a2: It is banned in several countries
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q2a3: It can only be served in copper mugs
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q2a4: It requires a special bartender license
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q2exp: The Dark 'n' Stormy is a registered trademark of Gosling's — it can officially only be made with Gosling's Black Seal rum.
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q3: What is the most popular tequila cocktail in Mexico?
academy.cocktail.l1.les2.q3exp: The Paloma (tequila + grapefruit + soda) is the most consumed tequila cocktail in Mexico, surpassing even the Margarita.
academy.cocktail.l2.title: Sours & Daisies
academy.cocktail.l2.desc: Shaken cocktails, citrus balance, and egg white
academy.cocktail.l2.t1: The Sour is one of the oldest cocktail families: spirit + citrus + sweet. The classic ratio is 2:1:1 (60ml spirit, 30ml citrus, 30ml sweet) or the 'Golden Ratio' 2:¾:¾. The acid-sweet balance is the key.
academy.cocktail.l2.tip1: Always use freshly squeezed juice. Bottled juice contains preservatives that alter the flavor. Lemon juice lasts 4 hours max; lime juice, 8 hours.
academy.cocktail.l2.note1: Egg white transforms a sour: it adds silky texture and foam. Use the 'dry shake' technique (shake without ice first), then 'wet shake' (with ice). The result is a creamy, stable foam.
academy.cocktail.l2.t2: The sour template allows infinite variations by swapping each component: Whiskey Sour (bourbon), Daiquiri (rum + lime), Margarita (tequila + lime + triple sec), Gimlet (gin + lime). Same concept, different spirits.
academy.cocktail.l2.tip2: For a perfect Daiquiri: 60ml white rum, 22ml lime, 15ml syrup. Shake vigorously for 12 seconds. Double-strain into a chilled coupe. Do not add fruit or serve it frozen — that is a different drink.
academy.cocktail.l2.t3: A Daisy is a sour that uses a liqueur as the sweetener instead of simple syrup. The Margarita is a tequila Daisy (in fact, 'margarita' means 'daisy' in Spanish). The Sidecar is a cognac Daisy with Cointreau.
academy.cocktail.l2.note2: The Pisco Sour includes egg white and Angostura as decoration on the foam. The bitters are not mixed in: they are dropped onto the foam and a pattern is drawn with a toothpick.
academy.cocktail.l2.t4: Modern sours explore alternative sweeteners: honey (Gold Rush, Bee's Knees), honey-ginger syrup (Penicillin), agave (Tommy's Margarita). Each sweetener brings its own character to the cocktail's balance.
academy.cocktail.l2.tip3: The Penicillin uses a float of smoky Islay whisky at the end. This 'float' is poured gently over a spoon so it sits on the surface, creating a smoky aroma before each sip.
academy.cocktail.l2.q1: What is the classic ratio of a Sour?
academy.cocktail.l2.q1exp: The classic sour ratio is 2:1:1 — 2 parts spirit, 1 part citrus, and 1 part sweet.
academy.cocktail.l2.q2: What technique is used to create foam with egg white?
academy.cocktail.l2.q2a1: Dry shake (no ice) + wet shake (with ice)
academy.cocktail.l2.q2exp: The dry shake (without ice first) emulsifies the egg white; then the wet shake (with ice) chills and dilutes.
academy.cocktail.l2.q3a1: A sour with a liqueur as the sweetener
academy.cocktail.l2.q3exp: A Daisy is a sour that uses a liqueur (Cointreau, maraschino, etc.) as the sweetener instead of simple syrup.
academy.cocktail.l2.q4: Which cocktail is essentially a 'tequila Daisy'?
academy.cocktail.l2.q4exp: 'Margarita' means 'daisy' in Spanish. It is a tequila sour with triple sec as the sweetener.
academy.cocktail.l2.q5: How long does fresh lemon juice last for mixology?
academy.cocktail.l2.q5exp: Fresh lemon juice loses its properties after 4 hours. Lime juice lasts a bit longer, up to 8 hours.
academy.cocktail.l2.q6: What sweetener does the Gold Rush use instead of simple syrup?
academy.cocktail.l2.q6exp: The Gold Rush substitutes the Whiskey Sour's simple syrup with honey syrup, adding depth.
academy.cocktail.l2.q7: What spirit does the classic Daiquiri contain?
academy.cocktail.l2.q7exp: The classic Daiquiri contains white rum, fresh lime juice, and simple syrup. No fruit, no frozen.
academy.cocktail.l2.q8: How is Angostura applied in a Pisco Sour?
academy.cocktail.l2.q8a1: Dropped onto the foam as decoration
academy.cocktail.l2.q8a3: At the bottom of the glass
academy.cocktail.l2.q8exp: The Angostura is dropped onto the egg white foam and a pattern is drawn with a toothpick. It is not mixed in.
academy.cocktail.l2.q9: What whisky does the Penicillin use as a 'float'?
academy.cocktail.l2.q9exp: The Penicillin features a float of smoky Islay whisky (such as Lagavulin) on the surface of the cocktail.
academy.cocktail.l2.q10: Which cocktail family includes the Sidecar, Margarita, and Cosmopolitan?
academy.cocktail.l2.q10exp: They are all Daisies: sours that use a liqueur as the sweetener (Cointreau, triple sec).
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q1: What is the Golden Ratio for a Sour?
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q1exp: The Golden Ratio for sours is 2:¾:¾, producing a slightly drier and more spirit-forward result than the classic 2:1:1.
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q2: Why must you always use fresh juice in sours?
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q2a1: Bottled juice has preservatives that alter the flavor
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q2a4: Fresh juice has a nicer color
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q2exp: Bottled juice contains preservatives that alter the flavor profile. Fresh lemon juice lasts only 4 hours max for optimal taste.
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q3: How long does fresh lemon juice remain viable for cocktails?
academy.cocktail.l2.les0.q3exp: Fresh lemon juice loses its balanced flavor after 4 hours. Lime juice lasts slightly longer, up to 8 hours.
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q1: What base spirit does a classic Daiquiri use?
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q1exp: The classic Daiquiri uses white rum with fresh lime juice and simple syrup — no fruit, no frozen.
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q2: What citrus does a Gimlet use?
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q2exp: The Gimlet combines gin with lime juice (and traditionally lime cordial), making it a gin-based sour.
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q3: What technique creates the foam in an egg white sour?
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q3a1: Dry shake first, then wet shake with ice
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q3a2: Blend with ice in a blender
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q3a3: Stir vigorously in a mixing glass
academy.cocktail.l2.les1.q3exp: A dry shake (without ice) first emulsifies the egg white to create foam, then a wet shake (with ice) chills and dilutes.
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q1: What makes a Daisy different from a standard Sour?
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q1a1: It uses a liqueur as the sweetener instead of simple syrup
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q1a4: It is stirred instead of shaken
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q1exp: A Daisy is a sour that replaces simple syrup with a liqueur (like Cointreau or triple sec) as the sweetener.
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q2: The Sidecar is a Daisy made with which base spirit?
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q2exp: The Sidecar is a cognac Daisy with Cointreau as the sweetening liqueur.
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q3: How is Angostura bitters applied in a Pisco Sour?
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q3a1: Dropped onto the egg white foam as decoration
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q3a3: Muddled at the bottom of the glass
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q3a4: It is not used in a Pisco Sour
academy.cocktail.l2.les2.q3exp: In a Pisco Sour, Angostura bitters are dropped onto the egg white foam and a pattern is drawn with a toothpick.
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q1: What sweetener does Tommy's Margarita use instead of triple sec?
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q1exp: Tommy's Margarita replaces triple sec with agave syrup, letting the tequila shine with a cleaner agave-forward sweetness.
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q2: What unique syrup does the Penicillin cocktail use?
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q2exp: The Penicillin uses honey-ginger syrup combined with blended Scotch, finished with an Islay whisky float for smokiness.
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q3: What do the Gold Rush and Bee's Knees have in common?
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q3a1: Both use honey as the sweetener
academy.cocktail.l2.les3.q3exp: Both the Gold Rush and the Bee's Knees use honey syrup as their sweetener instead of simple syrup, adding depth and floral notes.
academy.cocktail.l3.title: Spirit-Forward
academy.cocktail.l3.desc: Martini, Manhattan, Negroni, Old Fashioned, and stirred cocktails
academy.cocktail.l3.les0: The Old Fashioned and its variations
academy.cocktail.l3.t1: Spirit-forward cocktails let the spirit shine. They use little or no citrus and are prepared stirred in a mixing glass. Controlled dilution and temperature are crucial. Large ice is essential when serving.
academy.cocktail.l3.tip1: When stirring, the spoon should glide gently along the wall of the mixing glass. The motion comes from the fingers, not the wrist. Goal: chill and dilute without aerating.
academy.cocktail.l3.note1: The Old Fashioned is the oldest cocktail in existence — it IS the original 'cocktail.' Its recipe (spirit + sugar + bitters + water) defines the entire category. Everything else came after.
academy.cocktail.l3.t2: The Manhattan (whiskey + sweet vermouth + bitters) established the pattern for dozens of variations: Rob Roy (Scotch), Boulevardier (with Campari), Black Manhattan (with Amaro Averna). Changing one ingredient creates a new cocktail.
academy.cocktail.l3.tip2: Vermouth is a fortified wine. Once opened, it oxidizes like any wine. Store it in the refrigerator and use it within 4–6 weeks. Stale vermouth ruins any cocktail.
academy.cocktail.l3.t3: The Dry Martini is the most debated cocktail: the gin/vermouth ratio has varied from 1:1 to nearly straight gin. 'Dry' means less vermouth. A 'wet' Martini has more vermouth. 'Dirty' adds olive brine.
academy.cocktail.l3.note2: The Sazerac is the official cocktail of New Orleans. It is prepared with an absinthe 'rinse': the glass is rinsed with absinthe and the excess is discarded. Only a whisper of anise remains.
academy.cocktail.l3.t4: The Negroni (gin + Campari + sweet vermouth) in equal parts is the gateway to bitter cocktails. The Boulevardier replaces the gin with bourbon. The Vieux Carré adds Bénédictine to the Manhattan, creating extra complexity.
academy.cocktail.l3.tip3: For spirit-forward garnish: the citrus twist is expressed over the cocktail to release essential oils, then rubbed along the rim of the glass. The oils from the twist are an ingredient, not just decoration.
academy.cocktail.l3.q1: What is the technique for preparing spirit-forward cocktails?
academy.cocktail.l3.q1exp: Spirit-forward cocktails are stirred in a mixing glass to chill without aerating, preserving the silky texture.
academy.cocktail.l3.q2: What are the 3 ingredients of a Negroni?
academy.cocktail.l3.q2exp: The Negroni is made with equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet red vermouth.
academy.cocktail.l3.q3: What does 'Dry' mean in a Dry Martini?
academy.cocktail.l3.q3exp: 'Dry' in a Martini means using less vermouth. The drier it is, the more the gin dominates.
academy.cocktail.l3.q4: How should vermouth be stored once opened?
academy.cocktail.l3.q4a4: It doesn't matter how it's stored
academy.cocktail.l3.q4exp: Vermouth is a fortified wine and oxidizes once opened. It must be refrigerated and used within 4–6 weeks.
academy.cocktail.l3.q5: Which cocktail is essentially a Negroni with bourbon instead of gin?
academy.cocktail.l3.q5exp: The Boulevardier replaces the Negroni's gin with bourbon or rye whiskey.
academy.cocktail.l3.q6: What special technique does the Sazerac use?
academy.cocktail.l3.q6exp: The Sazerac uses an absinthe 'rinse': the glass is rinsed and the excess is discarded, leaving only a whisper of anise.
academy.cocktail.l3.q7: What is the Old Fashioned in the history of mixology?
academy.cocktail.l3.q7a1: The original cocktail that defined the category
academy.cocktail.l3.q7exp: The Old Fashioned (spirit + sugar + bitters + water) is literally the original recipe of the 'cocktail.'
academy.cocktail.l3.q8: Why is the citrus twist expressed over a spirit-forward cocktail?
academy.cocktail.l3.q8a2: To add acidity to the cocktail
academy.cocktail.l3.q8a4: To change the color of the cocktail
academy.cocktail.l3.q8exp: The twist releases essential oils from the citrus peel, which add aroma to the cocktail. They are an ingredient, not just decoration.
academy.cocktail.l3.q9: What spirit does the Rob Roy contain?
academy.cocktail.l3.q9exp: The Rob Roy is a Manhattan made with Scotch Whisky instead of bourbon or rye. It is the 'Scottish Manhattan.'
academy.cocktail.l3.q10: What herbal liqueur does the Vieux Carré add to the Manhattan pattern?
academy.cocktail.l3.q10exp: The Vieux Carré adds Bénédictine to the Manhattan framework, creating a more complex cocktail with honey notes.
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q1: Why are spirit-forward cocktails stirred instead of shaken?
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q1a1: To chill and dilute without aerating
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q1exp: Spirit-forward cocktails are stirred to achieve controlled dilution and temperature while preserving a silky, clear texture without aeration.
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q2: What are the four components of an Old Fashioned?
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q2exp: The Old Fashioned (spirit + sugar + bitters + water) is the original cocktail recipe that defined the entire category.
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q3: Where should the stirring motion come from when making a spirit-forward cocktail?
academy.cocktail.l3.les0.q3exp: The stirring motion should come from the fingers, not the wrist, allowing the spoon to glide gently along the wall of the mixing glass.
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q1: What are the three ingredients of a Manhattan?
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q1a3: Bourbon, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q1exp: The Manhattan combines whiskey with sweet vermouth and bitters, establishing a pattern for dozens of variations.
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q2: How long does vermouth last once opened, if properly refrigerated?
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q2exp: Vermouth is a fortified wine that oxidizes once opened. It must be refrigerated and used within 4-6 weeks.
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q3: What is the ratio of ingredients in a Negroni?
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q3a1: Equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q3a2: 2 parts gin, 1 part Campari, 1 part vermouth
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q3a3: 3 parts gin, 1 part Campari, 1 part vermouth
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q3a4: 1 part gin, 2 parts Campari, 1 part vermouth
academy.cocktail.l3.les1.q3exp: The Negroni uses equal parts of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth — a perfectly balanced three-way split.
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q1: What does 'dirty' mean in a Dirty Martini?
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q1a3: It is served at room temperature
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q1exp: A 'dirty' Martini includes olive brine, which adds a savory, briny character to the drink.
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q2: What is an absinthe rinse in a Sazerac?
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q2a1: The glass is coated with absinthe and the excess is discarded
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q2a2: Absinthe is mixed into the cocktail as a main ingredient
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q2a3: The ice cubes are soaked in absinthe
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q2a4: Absinthe is floated on top of the cocktail
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q2exp: In a Sazerac, the glass is rinsed with absinthe and the excess is discarded, leaving only a whisper of anise flavor.
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q3: What are the two main ingredients of a Dry Martini?
academy.cocktail.l3.les2.q3exp: The classic Dry Martini combines gin with dry vermouth, stirred and strained. 'Dry' indicates less vermouth.
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q1a1: A Negroni with bourbon instead of gin
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q1a2: A Manhattan with Campari instead of bitters
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q1a3: A Martini with Scotch instead of gin
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q1exp: The Boulevardier replaces the Negroni's gin with bourbon, creating a richer, warmer variation of the classic.
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q2: What does the Vieux Carré add to the Manhattan formula?
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q2exp: The Vieux Carré adds Bénédictine to the Manhattan framework, creating a more complex cocktail with honey and herbal notes.
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q3: Why is a citrus twist expressed over a spirit-forward cocktail?
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q3a1: To release essential oils that add aroma — it is an ingredient, not just decoration
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q3a2: To add citrus juice to the cocktail
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q3a4: To change the color of the drink
academy.cocktail.l3.les3.q3exp: The citrus twist is expressed to release essential oils over the cocktail. These oils are a functional ingredient adding aroma, not merely decoration.
academy.cocktail.l4.title: Tropical & Tiki
academy.cocktail.l4.desc: Multi-spirit, exotic ingredients, blending, and tiki
academy.cocktail.l4.t1: Tiki culture was born in the 1930s with Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic in California. Their philosophy: use multiple rums, tropical juices, and exotic syrups to create complex, impossible-to-guess flavors. Recipes were secret, with coded ingredients.
academy.cocktail.l4.note1: Trader Vic and Don the Beachcomber disputed the invention of the Mai Tai for decades. Trader Vic won the debate, but both profoundly influenced tiki culture.
academy.cocktail.l4.tip1: Tiki cocktails typically use 2–3 different rums (white, gold, dark/Demerara). Each rum contributes different notes: white brings cleanliness, gold brings depth, and Demerara brings caramelized richness.
academy.cocktail.l4.t2: Essential tiki ingredients: Falernum (lime, clove, almond), Orgeat (almond), Allspice Dram (allspice), Coconut cream, Tropical juices (pineapple, passion fruit, grapefruit). Many tiki recipes are secret and use the bar's own proprietary 'mixes.'
academy.cocktail.l4.tip2: The tiki 'flash blend' uses a blender with crushed ice for only 5 seconds — it is not a frozen daiquiri. The goal is to integrate and chill, not make a smoothie. The result should have a granita-like texture.
academy.cocktail.l4.t3: The Planter's Punch follows the mnemonic rule: 'One of Sour, Two of Sweet, Three of Strong, Four of Weak' (1 part citrus, 2 sweet, 3 rum, 4 ice/water). The Singapore Sling started the trend of long, fruity tropical cocktails.
academy.cocktail.l4.note2: Tiki garnishes are part of the experience: tiny umbrellas, carved fruit, edible orchids, and literal fire (with overproof rum). Tiki is liquid theater.
academy.cocktail.l4.q1: Who are the two founding fathers of tiki culture?
academy.cocktail.l4.q1a1: Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic
academy.cocktail.l4.q1exp: Don the Beachcomber (Ernest Gantt) and Trader Vic (Victor Bergeron) founded tiki culture in California in the 1930s.
academy.cocktail.l4.q2: How many rums do tiki cocktails typically use?
academy.cocktail.l4.q2exp: Tiki cocktails typically blend 2–3 rums of different styles to create flavor complexity.
academy.cocktail.l4.q3a1: A syrup/liqueur of lime, clove, and almond
academy.cocktail.l4.q3exp: Falernum is a Caribbean syrup or liqueur made with lime, clove, almond, and spices. It is essential in tiki cocktails.
academy.cocktail.l4.q4: What is the mnemonic rule for Planter's Punch?
academy.cocktail.l4.q4exp: 'One of Sour, Two of Sweet, Three of Strong, Four of Weak' is the classic Planter's Punch rule.
academy.cocktail.l4.q5: Which tiki cocktail introduced Campari to the tropical world?
academy.cocktail.l4.q5exp: The Jungle Bird, created in 1978 at the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, broke the mold by combining Campari with rum and tropical juices.
academy.cocktail.l4.q6: What is the 'flash blend' in tiki?
academy.cocktail.l4.q6a1: Blending with ice for only 5 seconds
academy.cocktail.l4.q6exp: The flash blend means blending with crushed ice for only 5 seconds, creating a granita-like texture without making a smoothie.
academy.cocktail.l4.q7: What does the name 'Three Dots and a Dash' mean in Morse code?
academy.cocktail.l4.q7exp: Three Dots and a Dash (· · · —) is Morse code for V, for Victory. It was created by Don the Beachcomber during WWII.
academy.cocktail.l4.q8: What ingredient contributes almond notes in tiki cocktails?
academy.cocktail.l4.q8exp: Orgeat is an almond syrup with orange flower water that contributes almond and marzipan notes to cocktails.
academy.cocktail.l4.q9exp: The Painkiller was created at the Soggy Dollar Bar in the Virgin Islands, where patrons would swim to the bar.
academy.cocktail.l4.q10: What rum does the Barbadian Corn 'n' Oil use?
academy.cocktail.l4.q10exp: Corn 'n' Oil uses blackstrap rum (dark, dense rum) with falernum. Its name describes its dark, oily appearance.
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q1: In what decade did tiki culture originate?
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q1exp: Tiki culture was born in the 1930s in California, founded by Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic.
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q2: Why were tiki recipes originally kept secret?
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q2a1: They used coded ingredients to prevent copying
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q2a4: They were too simple to patent
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q2exp: Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic used coded ingredient names in their recipes to prevent competitors from copying their drinks.
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q3: Who is generally credited with inventing the Mai Tai after a long dispute?
academy.cocktail.l4.les0.q3exp: Trader Vic and Don the Beachcomber disputed the Mai Tai's authorship for decades; Trader Vic generally won the debate.
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q1: Why do tiki cocktails use multiple rums?
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q1a1: Each rum contributes different flavor notes for complexity
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q1a3: Because a single rum would be too sweet
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q1a4: It is required by tiki tradition but has no practical purpose
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q1exp: Tiki cocktails blend 2-3 rums (white, gold, Demerara) because each brings different notes: cleanliness, depth, and caramelized richness.
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q2exp: Orgeat is an almond syrup (often with orange flower water) used in tiki cocktails like the Mai Tai for almond and marzipan notes.
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q3: How long does a tiki 'flash blend' last?
academy.cocktail.l4.les1.q3exp: The flash blend uses a blender with crushed ice for only 5 seconds — just enough to integrate and chill without making a smoothie.
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q1: What is the mnemonic formula for Planter's Punch?
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q1exp: The classic Planter's Punch follows 'One of Sour, Two of Sweet, Three of Strong, Four of Weak' as its ratio formula.
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q2: What role do garnishes play in tiki cocktails?
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q2a1: They are part of the full tiki experience
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q2a2: They are purely optional and decorative
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q2a3: They are only used in competitions
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q2a4: They replace the need for bitters
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q2exp: Tiki garnishes (umbrellas, carved fruit, fire) are part of the experience — tiki is 'liquid theater' where presentation matters.
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q3: What cocktail started the trend of long, fruity tropical drinks?
academy.cocktail.l4.les2.q3exp: The Singapore Sling started the trend of long, fruity tropical cocktails and influenced the tiki movement.
academy.cocktail.l5.title: Advanced Techniques
academy.cocktail.l5.desc: Flips, Punches, Cobblers, Fizzes, and modern techniques
academy.cocktail.l5.t1: The Fizz is a sour served with soda. The Ramos Gin Fizz is its masterpiece: gin + citrus + egg white + cream + orange flower water, shaken for 12+ minutes (historically) to create an impossibly silky foam. Today a dry shake + extended wet shake is used.
academy.cocktail.l5.tip1: For a modern Ramos Gin Fizz: dry shake 30 seconds without ice, then wet shake 2 minutes with ice. Pour into a glass with no ice and slowly add the soda — you'll see the foam rise above the rim like a soufflé.
academy.cocktail.l5.note1: Henry C. Ramos employed teams of 'shaker boys' at his New Orleans bar. Each bartender would shake for minutes and pass the shaker to the next. It was said the sound could be heard a block away.
academy.cocktail.l5.t2: A Flip contains a whole egg (yolk + white), spirit, and sugar, with no citrus. The result is creamy and rich. A Cobbler is spirit + fresh fruit + sugar over crushed ice. Punches are the mothers of all cocktails: batch versions meant for sharing.
academy.cocktail.l5.tip2: For a perfect Flip: use a fresh whole egg, vigorous dry shake, then wet shake. Freshly grated nutmeg at the end is essential — it adds a spiced aroma that complements the creaminess.
academy.cocktail.l5.t3: The Brandy Crusta (1850s, New Orleans) is considered the grandmother of sours. Its sugar 'crusta' and the complete lemon peel inside the glass were revolutionary. The Last Word resurfaced in 2004 after decades of obscurity — a perfect equal-parts cocktail.
academy.cocktail.l5.note2: The cocktail renaissance of the 2000s rediscovered dozens of forgotten recipes. Bartenders like Murray Stenson (Last Word), Sam Ross (Penicillin), and Audrey Saunders (Gin-Gin Mule) created modern classics worthy of the originals.
academy.cocktail.l5.t4: Champagne cocktails: the French 75 (gin + lemon + sugar + champagne) is the star. The base is shaken and topped with cold champagne. The Gin Fizz marked the transition between classic and modern mixology with its refined foam and carbonation technique.
academy.cocktail.l5.tip3: When making champagne cocktails, never shake the champagne — it loses its bubbles. Only shake the base (spirit + citrus + sweet) and top with cold champagne directly in the glass.
academy.cocktail.l5.q1: How long was the Ramos Gin Fizz historically shaken?
academy.cocktail.l5.q1exp: The Ramos Gin Fizz was historically shaken for 12+ minutes to achieve its iconic foam. Today a dry shake + extended wet shake is used.
academy.cocktail.l5.q2: What distinguishes a Flip from a Sour?
academy.cocktail.l5.q2a1: It contains a whole egg and no citrus
academy.cocktail.l5.q2exp: A Flip uses a whole egg (yolk + white), spirit, and sugar, but no citrus. It is creamy and rich, not acidic.
academy.cocktail.l5.q3: Which cocktail from the 1850s is considered the 'grandmother of sours'?
academy.cocktail.l5.q3exp: The Brandy Crusta (1850s, New Orleans) introduced the sugar crusta and the lemon peel, being the precursor to all sours.
academy.cocktail.l5.q4: What special ingredient does the Ramos Gin Fizz contain besides egg white?
academy.cocktail.l5.q4exp: The Ramos Gin Fizz contains cream and orange flower water, in addition to the egg white.
academy.cocktail.l5.q5a1: Spirit + fresh fruit + sugar over crushed ice
academy.cocktail.l5.q5exp: A Cobbler is served over crushed ice with fresh fruit and sugar. It was the cocktail that popularized the use of the straw.
academy.cocktail.l5.q6: Who rediscovered the Last Word in 2004?
academy.cocktail.l5.q6exp: Murray Stenson, a Seattle bartender, rediscovered the Last Word from a forgotten 1916 recipe and brought it back to fame.
academy.cocktail.l5.q7: How is champagne added in a French 75?
academy.cocktail.l5.q7a1: Topped at the end, without shaking
academy.cocktail.l5.q7exp: The base is shaken separately (gin + lemon + sugar) and topped with cold champagne directly in the glass to preserve the bubbles.
academy.cocktail.l5.q8: What spice is grated as a final garnish on a Flip?
academy.cocktail.l5.q8exp: Freshly grated nutmeg is the classic garnish for a Flip, complementing the creaminess of the egg.
academy.cocktail.l5.q9: What are Punches in the history of mixology?
academy.cocktail.l5.q9a1: The mothers of all cocktails, prepared in batches
academy.cocktail.l5.q9exp: Punches are the ancestors of mixology: batch drinks meant for sharing, predating the individual cocktail.
academy.cocktail.l5.q10: What modern technique is used today for the Ramos Gin Fizz?
academy.cocktail.l5.q10exp: Today a dry shake of 30 seconds (without ice) is done to emulsify, followed by a wet shake of 2 minutes with ice to chill and dilute.
academy.cocktail.l5.les0.q1exp: A Fizz is a sour (spirit + citrus + sweet) topped with soda water for effervescence.
academy.cocktail.l5.les0.q2: What ingredients make the Ramos Gin Fizz unique compared to a regular Gin Fizz?
academy.cocktail.l5.les0.q2exp: The Ramos Gin Fizz adds cream and orange flower water to the standard fizz formula, creating its legendary silky foam.
academy.cocktail.l5.les0.q3: In the modern technique for a Ramos Gin Fizz, how long is the dry shake?
academy.cocktail.l5.les0.q3exp: The modern technique calls for a 30-second dry shake (without ice) to emulsify, followed by a 2-minute wet shake with ice.
academy.cocktail.l5.les1.q1a1: Whole egg + spirit + sugar, no citrus
academy.cocktail.l5.les1.q1exp: A Flip uses a whole egg (yolk and white) with spirit and sugar but never contains citrus, resulting in a creamy, rich drink.
academy.cocktail.l5.les1.q2: What is the classic garnish for a Flip?
academy.cocktail.l5.les1.q2exp: Freshly grated nutmeg is the traditional Flip garnish, adding a spiced aroma that complements the egg's creaminess.
academy.cocktail.l5.les1.q3: What are Punches in the context of cocktail history?
academy.cocktail.l5.les1.q3exp: Punches are batch drinks made for sharing and predate the individual cocktail — they are the ancestors of modern mixology.
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q1: When was the Brandy Crusta created?
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q1exp: The Brandy Crusta was created in the 1850s in New Orleans and is considered the grandmother of sours.
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q2: What makes the Brandy Crusta distinctive in its presentation?
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q2a1: A sugar crusta on the rim and a full lemon peel inside the glass
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q2exp: The Brandy Crusta features a sugar-crusted rim and an entire lemon peel lining the inside of the glass — revolutionary for its time.
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q3: In what year was the Last Word rediscovered by Murray Stenson?
academy.cocktail.l5.les2.q3exp: Murray Stenson, a Seattle bartender, rediscovered the Last Word from a forgotten recipe and brought it back to fame in 2004.
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q1: What is the base spirit of a French 75?
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q1exp: The French 75 combines gin with lemon juice, sugar, and champagne. The name refers to a French 75mm field gun.
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q2: Why should you never shake champagne when making a champagne cocktail?
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q2a2: It makes the drink too cold
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q2a3: It causes the bottle to explode
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q2a4: It changes the flavor of the champagne
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q2exp: Shaking champagne destroys its carbonation. Only the base (spirit + citrus + sweet) is shaken, then topped with cold champagne.
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q3: What is the correct method for preparing a French 75?
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q3a1: Shake the base, then top with cold champagne in the glass
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q3a2: Stir everything together in a mixing glass
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q3a3: Shake all ingredients including the champagne
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q3a4: Build directly in the glass without shaking
academy.cocktail.l5.les3.q3exp: The base (gin + lemon + sugar) is shaken with ice and strained, then topped with cold champagne directly in the glass.

wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.sub: Crystal-clear cocktails with no pulp or particles
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.descri: Double straining is an essential technique for crystal-clear cocktails with a clean mouthfeel, removing ice shards, pulp, herbs, seeds, and other solids. You strain the cocktail TWICE simultaneously: first through a hawthorne strainer (on the shaker), then through a fine mesh strainer held over the serving glass. The result is a silky texture and flawless presentation.
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.how: 1) Shake the cocktail normally with ice. 2) Place the hawthorne strainer on top of the shaker. 3) Hold the fine mesh strainer with your left hand OVER the serving glass. 4) With your right hand, pour the cocktail through both strainers at once in one fluid motion. 5) Tilt slightly to speed up the flow. The drink passes hawthorne → fine mesh → glass, removing every solid before it hits the glass.
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.tips: Always use a FINE mesh strainer (not a regular one) — coarse mesh lets small particles through. The best ones are stainless steel with very tight mesh. Clean the fine strainer immediately after use — it clogs easily with pulp. Never press a spoon through the mesh (it pushes solids through). The correct technique is to let gravity do the work. A small investment ($15-30) for a huge difference in the cocktail's visual quality.
wiki.art.techniques.double-strain.when: Mandatory for shaken cocktails with muddled herbs (mint, basil, jalapeño), fresh fruit, egg white, or when using crushed ice in the shaker. Essential for: Margarita (lime pulp), Gin Basil Smash (basil leaves), Whiskey Sour (egg white foam), Daiquiri (lime pulp), any cocktail with fresh berries, tiki drinks with spices. Unnecessary in stirred drinks (Manhattan, Martini — no solids to strain).
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.descriptio: The dry shake is the technique of shaking a cocktail WITHOUT ice before the regular shake, to fully emulsify egg whites or aquafaba and create the dense, silky foam that defines Sours. Ice would chill the proteins prematurely and prevent proper emulsification. Two shakes: first dry (no ice) to emulsify, then with ice to chill and dilute.
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.how: STANDARD METHOD: 1) Add all ingredients (including the egg white) to the shaker WITHOUT ice. 2) Shake vigorously for 10-15 seconds (no ice, a muted sound). 3) Open, add ice. 4) Shake again 10-15 seconds with ice (bright metallic sound). 5) Double-strain into the glass. REVERSE DRY SHAKE: shake FIRST with ice, strain the ice out, then dry shake the already chilled liquid — produces even denser foam.
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.tips: For perfect foam: use FRESH egg white (ideally unpasteurized). Aquafaba (canned chickpea liquid) is an identical vegan substitute. Adding a small hawthorne spring inside the shaker during the dry shake speeds up emulsification — 5-7 seconds is enough. For the iconic Angostura "painting": dry shake → ice → shake → double-strain → dashes of Angostura on the foam → use a toothpick to draw. Without a dry shake, the modern Whiskey Sour is impossible.
wiki.art.techniques.dry-shake.when: Mandatory in any cocktail with egg white or aquafaba: Whiskey Sour, Pisco Sour, Gin Sour, Ramos Gin Fizz, Clover Club, Pink Lady, Aviation with egg, Whiskey Fix. Without a dry shake, the foam is thin and short-lived. Also useful for cocktails with whipped cream or pasteurized whites. Unnecessary for cocktails without proteins (most modern sours use the technique).
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.sub: Infusing fats to add texture and flavor
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.description: Fat-washing is a modern technique that infuses a spirit with animal or vegetable fats to add flavor and a silky texture. The fat is mixed with the alcohol at room temperature, frozen (the fat solidifies), and removed — leaving the fat-soluble aromatics in the spirit while eliminating the fat itself. The result: a spirit with unique character and silky mouthfeel. It is the most revolutionary technique of 2000s modern bartending.
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.how: METHOD: 1) Render the fat (cook bacon to get liquid fat, or melt butter). 2) Mix 60ml of rendered fat with 750ml of spirit at room temperature in a container. 3) Shake to emulsify. 4) Let stand 4 hours at room temperature — aromatic molecules transfer to the alcohol. 5) Freeze for 12-24h — the fat solidifies on the surface. 6) Strain through a coffee filter (or mesh + cheesecloth) to remove all fat. The resulting spirit is clear and clean but with transformed flavor and texture.
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.tips: Standard ratio: 60ml fat per 750ml spirit (adjust to desired intensity). Liquid fats at room temperature (oils) only need refrigeration (4h), not freezing. Solid fats (bacon, butter) require deep freezing. Filter TWICE with a coffee filter for crystal-clear results. Fat-washed spirits keep for months refrigerated. Bacon + bourbon + maple syrup = Benton's Old Fashioned, the cocktail that launched the technique. Experiment with olive oil + gin, coconut oil + rum, duck fat + cognac.
wiki.art.techniques.fat-wash.when: Use it to create unique spirits with flavors unattainable any other way: Bacon-washed bourbon (Benton's Old Fashioned, Don Lee 2007), coconut fat-washed rum, duck fat bourbon, butter-washed rum, sesame oil gin, olive oil gin (for textured Martinis). Best in stirred/refined cocktails where the silky mouthfeel shines (Old Fashioned, Manhattan). Invented by bartender Eben Freeman (Tailor NYC, 2006) and popularized by Don Lee.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.sub: Macerating ingredients in spirits to create unique flavors
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.description: Infusion is the technique of macerating ingredients (fruits, herbs, spices, chilies, tea, coffee) in a spirit for hours or days to transfer their flavors and aromas to the alcohol. It is one of the most versatile cocktail techniques — it allows you to create custom spirits you cannot buy. From classic jalapeño-infused tequila for spicy Margaritas to exotic herbal infusions, it expands the bartender's repertoire infinitely.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.how: APPROXIMATE TIMES by ingredient: Fresh chilies (jalapeño, habanero): 2-4 hours. Fresh herbs (basil, rosemary): 1-2 hours (longer turns bitter). Tea: 10-30 minutes (longer becomes tannic). Soft fruits (strawberry, peach): 24-48 hours. Whole spices (cinnamon, clove): 2-7 days. Coffee: 12-24 hours. Vanilla: 1-2 weeks. METHOD: cut ingredient into pieces, add to spirit in a sealed jar, store cool and dark, taste daily, strain once you hit desired intensity. Label with date and ingredient.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.tips: TASTE every 2-4 hours (chilies/herbs) or every 12-24h (fruits/spices) — over-infusion is irreversible. Chilies: remove seeds and white ribs to avoid extreme heat. Tea and tender herbs: do NOT exceed times — they go bitter quickly. Fruits: cut small for more contact area. For clear infusions, use neutral spirits (vodka, unaged); for complex infusions, spirits with character (bourbon, tequila, dark rum). ALWAYS label with date and content. They keep 2-4 weeks refrigerated.
wiki.art.techniques.infusion.when: Whenever you want a specific flavor in a spirit that doesn't exist commercially, or when quality/freshness beats any industrial product. Classic examples: Tequila + jalapeño (4h), Vodka + cucumber (24h), Gin + Earl Grey tea (2h), Bourbon + apple + cinnamon (48h), Rum + vanilla + coffee (1 week), Vodka + habanero (12h). Essential technique for creative bars and original cocktail menus. Also used for syrups, vinegars, and sauces.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.sub: The tiki technique with the Caribbean stick
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.description: The swizzle is a traditional Caribbean technique that uses a swizzle stick (bois lelé) to mix and chill cocktails directly in the serving glass full of crushed ice. By rotating the stick between the palms of your hands, you create turbulent motion that chills the cocktail without over-diluting, while the crushed ice builds the signature frost on the outside of the glass. It is the technique that defines the tiki style and classic tropical cocktails.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.how: 1) Build the cocktail directly in a highball/Collins glass. 2) Fill the glass COMPLETELY with crushed ice (not cubes). 3) Insert the swizzle stick to the bottom of the glass. 4) Rotate the stick rapidly between the palms of your hands in a friction motion — up and down, side to side, for 15-20 seconds. 5) The glass should frost over on the outside — the sign that it's cold enough. 6) Top up with more crushed ice. 7) Add bitters and garnish.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.tips: The traditional swizzle stick is the bois lelé (Quararibea turbinata tree) — its three split prongs at the base act as a natural whisk. Substitutes: long bar spoon (less effective), long-handled whisk. For perfect frost on the glass: press against the ice with a vertical motion, not circular. The Queen's Park Swizzle is the canonical example: gently muddled mint, lime, demerara sugar, dark rum, crushed ice, swizzle, Angostura on top. A technique that sets serious tiki bartenders apart.
wiki.art.techniques.swizzle.when: Essential for traditional tiki cocktails and Caribbean drinks with crushed ice: Queen's Park Swizzle (rum, mint, lime, sugar, bitters — Trinidad, 1915), Bermuda Rum Swizzle (various rums, juices, bitters), Gin-Gin Mule, tiki-style drinks from Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic. Also for any cocktail where you want the iconic exterior frost. Do not use for classic stirred cocktails (Martini, Manhattan) or for cocktails with egg white.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.descripti: The Sour family is THE MOST IMPORTANT STRUCTURE in classic and modern bartending. It rests on three pillars: spirit (base), acid (citrus), and sweet (syrup/liqueur). This simple trinity generates infinite variations: from the Whiskey Sour to the Margarita, Daiquiri, and Sidecar. Mastering the Sour is mastering bartending — any professional can build a cocktail on its template. The traditional Sour also includes egg white for silky texture.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.examples: WHISKEY SOUR (bourbon, lemon, syrup, egg white) — the prototype. MARGARITA (tequila, lime, Cointreau — Cointreau replaces the syrup). DAIQUIRI (white rum, lime, syrup). SIDECAR (cognac, Cointreau, lemon). PISCO SOUR (pisco, lime, syrup, egg white, Angostura). GIMLET (gin, lime cordial). SOUTHSIDE (gin, lime, syrup, mint). CLOVER CLUB (gin, raspberry, lemon, egg white). PAPER PLANE (bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, lemon — modern). PENICILLIN (scotch, lemon, honey-ginger, Islay float).
wiki.art.families.sours-family.origin: USA, 19th century. The term "sour" first appears in Jerry Thomas's "The Bon Vivant's Companion" (1862) as a cocktail category. Derived from British naval grog (rum + lime + sugar + water, to prevent scurvy), which Royal Navy sailors drank from 1740. The Whiskey Sour became the American standard by the 1870s-1880s and spread worldwide.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA: 60ml spirit + 22ml citrus juice (lemon/lime) + 15ml simple syrup. RATIO 2:¾:½, or David Embury's "Gold Standard" 8:3:2. Optional: egg white (20ml) or aquafaba for silky texture. To modify: citrus and syrup can be replaced by liqueurs that provide both (Cointreau is acid+sweet, Aperol is bitter+sweet). The Sour test: it should have a gentle acid kick on the first sip and a sweetness that accompanies, not dominates.
wiki.art.families.sours-family.tips: BALANCE: the 60/22/15 formula is a starting point — adjust for the spirit's intensity (overproof bourbon needs more acid/sweet; neutral vodka less). ALWAYS shake with ice to chill and aerate. Egg white transforms a sour into the modern silky-foam version (see dry-shake). SYRUP: simple (1:1) for clarity, demerara (2:1) for richness, diluted honey for depth. A perfect Whiskey Sour should be the first thing any new bartender masters — everything else derives from it.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.sub: Sours with bubbles — long and refreshing
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.descriptio: The Fizz is a variant of the Sour where soda water is added at the end, turning the short cocktail into a long, refreshing one. Typically served in a highball glass WITHOUT ice (maximum effervescence) or over ice. The name "fizz" is onomatopoeia for the sound of bubbling soda. The Gin Fizz is the prototype; the Ramos Gin Fizz is the category's masterpiece — a technical cocktail that requires 12 minutes of shaking.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.examples: GIN FIZZ (gin, lemon, syrup, soda). SILVER FIZZ (Gin Fizz + egg white — with foam). RAMOS GIN FIZZ (gin, lemon, lime, cream, egg white, orange flower water, sugar, soda — 12-minute shake). SLOE GIN FIZZ (sloe gin, lemon, syrup, soda). DIAMOND FIZZ (gin, lemon, sugar, champagne — instead of soda). MORNING GLORY FIZZ (scotch, lemon, syrup, egg white, absinthe, soda). ROYAL GIN FIZZ (Gin Fizz with a whole egg). NEW ORLEANS FIZZ = Ramos Gin Fizz.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.origin: New Orleans and San Francisco, second half of the 19th century. The Gin Fizz appears in Jerry Thomas's 1887 book. Henry Ramos creates the Ramos Gin Fizz at the Imperial Cabinet Saloon in New Orleans in 1888 — it becomes so popular the bar hired teams of shakers to shake cocktails in assembly-line fashion during Mardi Gras. In 1915, 35 "shaker boys" shook Ramos Gin Fizzes non-stop throughout Carnival.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.structure: FORMULA: Sour + soda at the end. Standard: 60ml spirit + 22ml citrus + 15ml syrup + egg white (optional) + 60-90ml soda. Shake vigorously WITHOUT the soda, strain into a highball glass (cold, traditionally without ice), and top with soda. Silver Fizz = with egg white. Golden Fizz = with yolk. Royal Fizz = with whole egg. Ramos Fizz = Silver Fizz + cream + orange flower water + lime (the only one using two citrus juices). The effervescence should last several minutes of sipping.
wiki.art.families.fizz-family.tips: RAMOS GIN FIZZ: dry shake 1 min, ice and shake 3 min (or 12 min traditional), strain into a chilled highball with no ice, top with soda VERY SLOWLY — the foam should rise above the rim forming a "head". Orange flower water (1-2 dashes) is essential — without it, it's not a Ramos. Serve without ice for maximum effervescence. If using ice, add it after pouring. Drink with a straw to enjoy the layers: creamy foam on top, icy liquid below.
wiki.art.families.flip-family.descriptio: The Flip is a family of sumptuous cocktails that combine spirit, sugar, and a WHOLE egg (yolk and white), shaken vigorously to create a creamy, custard-like drinkable texture. Finished with a grating of nutmeg, it is a classic dessert cocktail that nearly disappeared after Prohibition but was revived by the cocktail renaissance. Originally served hot with a red-hot iron (hence "flipped"), today Flips are prepared cold with a dry-shake technique.
wiki.art.families.flip-family.examples: PORTO FLIP (tawny port, cognac, whole egg, nutmeg — the standard). BRANDY FLIP (brandy, sugar, egg — Jerry Thomas original). SHERRY FLIP (oloroso sherry, sugar, egg). COFFEE FLIP (coffee, egg, sugar, rum — hot). RUM FLIP (dark rum, sugar, egg — traditional Caribbean). WHISKEY FLIP (rye or bourbon, sugar, egg). CHOCOLATE FLIP (crème de cacao, egg, rum). MODERN FLIP (any spirit, honey, whole egg, creative variants).
wiki.art.families.flip-family.origin: England, late 17th century. The first Flips appear in the 1690s in dockside taverns — a mix of beer, rum, and sugar heated with a red-hot iron (loggerhead) that bartenders plunged into the drink, "flipping" the brew as it warmed. 19th century: the form evolves with a whole egg and is served cold. 1862: Jerry Thomas documents several Flips in "The Bon Vivant's Companion". 1920s-1970s: they nearly vanish. 2000s-present: revival with the cocktail renaissance.
wiki.art.families.flip-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA: 60ml spirit + 15ml syrup + 1 whole egg. Dry shake (without ice) 10-15 seconds to emulsify, then shake with ice another 10-15 seconds. Double-strain into a small coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Garnish: freshly grated nutmeg on top. Variations: swap syrup for honey, add a splash of cream for extra richness, change the spirit. Can be HOT (served in mugs, toddy-style) or COLD (modern style, more common).
wiki.art.families.flip-family.tips: The modern Flip IS a dessert cocktail — serve after dinner, not as an aperitif. Use a FRESH whole egg (the yolk gives body, the white the foam). Dry shake is MANDATORY to emulsify properly. ALWAYS freshly grated nutmeg on top — the aroma defines the Flip. 10-year tawny port is the quintessential Flip. Guest worried about raw egg: use pasteurized egg (the result is virtually identical). Aquafaba does NOT work for Flips — the yolk is irreplaceable for the creamy body.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.sub: Mint + crushed ice — American Southern elegance
wiki.art.families.julep-family.descripti: The Julep is a traditional cocktail of the American South, built on four elements: spirit, fresh mint, sugar, and abundant crushed ice. It is traditionally served in a silver julep cup that frosts over on the outside — the silver conducts the cold from the crushed ice and creates an iconic tactile and visual experience. The Mint Julep is the official cocktail of the Kentucky Derby (over 120,000 are served every year) and the emblem of Southern hospitality.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.examples: MINT JULEP (bourbon, mint, sugar, crushed ice — the Kentucky prototype). COGNAC JULEP (cognac, mint, sugar — the original version before bourbon replaced it in the 1830s). PEACH JULEP (bourbon, mint, sugar, peach purée). CHAMPAGNE JULEP (mint, sugar, champagne — Jerry Thomas). PINEAPPLE JULEP (rum, mint, pineapple, sugar). GIN JULEP (gin, mint, sugar — modern twist). SMOKY JULEP (mezcal, mint, agave).
wiki.art.families.julep-family.origin: Eighteenth century, American South (Kentucky, Virginia, Maryland). The word "julep" derives from Arabic "julab" (rose water) via Persian and Latin. The first written references appear in 1785 in Philadelphia newspapers. 1830s: the Mint Julep is established as the signature cocktail of the South, associated with the planter aristocracy. 1938: Churchill Downs (home of the Kentucky Derby) names it the race's official cocktail. Today it is an untouchable cultural symbol of the Derby.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.structure: CLASSIC FORMULA: 60-75ml spirit + 8-10 fresh mint leaves + 15ml simple syrup (or 2 sugar cubes + splash of water) + abundant crushed ice. LIGHTLY muddle the mint with the syrup in the bottom of the julep cup. Add the spirit. Fill completely with crushed ice. Stir with a julep spoon until the cup frosts on the outside. Add MORE crushed ice to form a dome above the rim. Garnish: fresh mint bouquet, short straw.
wiki.art.families.julep-family.tips: SILVER CUP: traditional and functional — conducts the cold from the ice. If you don't have one, use a highball with plenty of crushed ice. CRUSHED ICE: essential (not cubes) — creates the surface that frosts. Buy an ice crusher or pound with a Lewis bag. MINT: do NOT muddle aggressively — just press gently to release the oils, never tear the leaves (they release bitter chlorophyll). The mint bouquet garnish goes near the straw — so you smell the mint with every sip. Use bourbon at 45-50% ABV minimum (the crushed ice dilutes a lot).
wiki.art.families.punch-family.sub: Bowl cocktails — the oldest social tradition
wiki.art.families.punch-family.descripti: Punch is the MOTHER OF ALL COCKTAILS — the oldest family in bartending, originating in the 17th century before the term "cocktail" even existed. It is prepared in a large bowl for sharing, with five classic components: spirit (strong), citrus (sour), sugar (sweet), water (weak), and spices (tea/bitters).
